mcqs.question: Why is full fine-tuning significantly more resource-intensive than just running inference on the same model?
options: It requires holding the model weights, gradients, and optimizer state in memory simultaneously, often 3-4x the model's size
It requires a completely different model architecture than the one used for inference
It can only run on CPUs, never on GPUs
It permanently increases the model's parameter count with each training run
mcqs.explanation: Training needs memory for the forward activations, backward gradients, and optimizer state (like Adam's moment estimates) on top of the weights themselves, multiplying the memory footprint well beyond inference. It uses the same architecture, runs on GPUs (in fact requires them at scale), and doesn't change parameter count.

mcqs.question: What is the key insight that makes LoRA work?
options: Neural networks cannot be fine-tuned without changing every weight
The weight update needed to adapt a pretrained model to a new task tends to have low intrinsic rank, so a small low-rank matrix pair can approximate it well
Freezing the base model prevents it from being used for inference at all
Low-rank matrices always train faster regardless of what they represent
mcqs.explanation: LoRA's core assumption, borne out empirically, is that the necessary change to adapt a model is low-rank — so a small A/B matrix pair can capture most of the needed adjustment without touching the full weight matrix. The base model still runs fine for inference (with the adapter added), and it's not simply that low-rank matrices are faster in general — it's that this specific structure suffices here.

mcqs.question: A team needs their assistant to consistently write in a specific persistent brand voice across thousands of daily calls, and prompting the style into the system prompt hasn't held up reliably. What's the most appropriate next step?
options: Switch to RAG, since the problem is about facts, not behavior
Increase the temperature to make output more consistent
Fine-tune (e.g. via LoRA) on examples of the target voice, since the problem is a persistent behavioral/style shift prompting isn't reliably holding
Add more few-shot examples to every single call indefinitely as the only fix
mcqs.explanation: This is a style/behavior problem, not a missing-facts problem, so RAG doesn't address it. Fine-tuning bakes the desired behavior into the weights so it holds without depending on prompt engineering every call. Increasing temperature adds randomness, which fights consistency; permanently paying the token cost of few-shot examples on every call is a valid stopgap but not the most appropriate long-term fix once prompting has plateaued.

mcqs.question: A model fine-tuned on a small, narrow dataset becomes excellent at that task but noticeably worse at general instruction-following it used to handle fine. What's this called, and what's a way to guard against it?
options: Overfitting to the vocabulary; fixed only by switching tokenizers
Emergent ability loss; this cannot be prevented at any dataset size
Prompt injection; mitigated with input sanitization
Catastrophic forgetting; mitigated with a broader dataset, lower learning rate, fewer epochs, or a lower LoRA rank
mcqs.explanation: This is catastrophic forgetting — narrow fine-tuning data can overwrite general capabilities the model previously had. Guardrails include broadening the dataset, using a gentler learning rate, fewer training epochs, or (with LoRA) keeping the adapter rank low so it can't overwrite too much. It's unrelated to tokenizer vocabulary, prompt injection, or emergent abilities.

mcqs.question: Why does QLoRA keep the frozen base model in 4-bit precision while training the LoRA adapters at higher precision?
options: The frozen weights never receive a gradient update, so low precision costs little accuracy while cutting memory dramatically, whereas the actively-trained adapters need more precision
4-bit weights train faster because they require no quantization or dequantization at all
It's required by the LoRA math and has nothing to do with memory savings
Higher precision adapters are needed because the base model is deleted after quantization
mcqs.explanation: Since the base weights are frozen and never updated, quantizing them to 4-bit sacrifices little while saving large amounts of memory; the small adapter matrices that do get trained keep higher precision because they're the part actually learning. Quantization does add a dequantize step (a small compute cost, not a speed win), it's an engineering choice for memory not a math requirement, and the base model isn't deleted — it's still used at inference.

mcqs.question: A multi-tenant SaaS product needs a lightly customized model per customer for hundreds of customers. Why do teams typically keep one frozen base model and swap LoRA adapters per request, rather than merging and deploying hundreds of full model copies?
options: Merged models can no longer be used for inference at all
LoRA adapters cannot be merged under any circumstances
Serving one shared base model with small swappable adapters avoids the memory and cost of hosting hundreds of full-size model copies
Merging is only possible with full fine-tuning, never with LoRA
mcqs.explanation: Keeping the base model shared and swapping small per-customer adapters in and out is far cheaper than hosting a full model copy per customer, which is why multi-tenant products favor this path. Merged models absolutely still run inference fine — merging is optional, not a one-way trip to being unusable — and merging is in fact possible with LoRA (that's exactly what folding A x B into the weight does).
